Analysis In this section, we overview the reasons we believe con- tribute to the reduction in catastrophic forgetting when widening the network. Although wide networks have higher capacity, similar to how it has been shown that wider net- works generalize well because of implicit regularization imposed by gradient descent (Jacot et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2019), we argue that the behavior of catastrophic forgetting cannot be reduced to capacity alone and we need to integrate learning dynamics. Here, we ﬁrst construct a simple exam- ple for a regression problem with squared loss to demon- strate this point. Informally, we have the following claim. Claim 4.1 (informal). Consider learning problems with input space Rd, output space R, and squared loss. Let F1 be the class of linear models that maps the input to the output and F2 be the class of two-layer linear networks (i.e., no nonlinear activation). Then, there exist two tasks such that when we train task 2 using gradient descent, if we use model class F1, the amount of forgetting for task 1 is strictly zero; whereas if we use model class F2, the amount of forgetting can be positive. We provide details of the construction of the two tasks in Appendix C. As we can see, the two model classes F1 and F2 have exactly the same capacity, i.e., F1 = F2, since there is no nonlinearity in F2. However, due to the use of gradient descent algorithm, the amount of forgetting for task 1 is different for the two model classes when training on task 2. Moreover, in Appendix C, we show that if the size of a hidden layer in F2 is not large enough, then the forgetting could be more severe. Intuitively, if the additional layer becomes a bottleneck that projects the input to a very low dimensional space, the information can be lost. While this example is a specially constructed one, we be- lieve it can be helpful towards understanding the beneﬁts of wide neural networks in continual learning. In particular, it shows that we have to take the commonly used gradi- ent descent algorithm into account when investigating this phenomenon. In Appendix B, we provide further empirical results regarding the signiﬁcance of the width of the ﬁrst layer. In the following, we dive deeper in this phenomenon and provide several potential explanations.Wide Neural Networks Forget Less Catastrophically 2 3 4 5 Tasks (t) 50 60 70 80 90 Angle between ∇Lt and ∇L1 Width 32 128 512 2048 (a) MLP on Rotated MNIST 2 5 10 15 20 Tasks (t) 65 70 75 80 85 90 Angle between ∇Lt and ∇L1 Width 1 2 4 8 (b) WRN on Split CIFAR-100 Figure 3.The angle between the gradients at the optimum of task 1,∇L1(w∗ 1), and between the optimum of subsequent taskst, ∇Lt(w∗ t ), for t >1. Wider networks remain closer to 90 degree (more orthogonal). 4.1. Increased Gradient Orthogonality Earlier works in continual learning (Farajtabar et al., 2020; Chaudhry et al., 2018; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017; Riemer et al., 2018) have focused on explicitly forcing the gradients of the new tasks to be orthogonal to those of the previous ones to reduce forgetting among the tasks. Here, we want to look at how the gradient directions of different tasks evolve as the continual learning experience progresses while the networks’ width increases. We ﬁrst establish why orthogonalizing the gradients of different tasks is a good continual learning strategy. Let us consider a two-task continual learning problem, and study the amount of forgetting for task 1 induced by one gradient descent step on task 2. Let W⊆ Rp be the model parameter space and Lt(w) : W↦→ R be the training loss function of the t-th task. Assuming that all the loss functions are differentiable, according to mean value theorem, we have the following simple observation. Claim 4.2. Let w′ = w −η∇L2(w). Then there exists ξ∈[0,1] such that L1(w′) −L1(w) = −η⟨∇L1(w−ξη∇L2(w)),∇L2(w)⟩. (4.1) As we can see, the left hand side of Eq. 4.1 is the increase in the loss of task 1, and the right hand side is related to the inner product of the gradient of L1 at w−ξη∇L2(w), and the gradient of L2 at w. Therefore, if the gradients of the two tasks are more orthogonal to each other, then when training on new tasks, the model forgets less about previous task. Formally, we have the following direct corollary. Claim 4.3. Suppose that for any w1,w2 ∈W with ∥w1 − w2∥2 ≤ηsupw∈W∥∇L2(w)∥2, we have |⟨∇L1(w1),∇L2(w2)⟩|≤ ϵ/η, for some ϵ> 0, and let w′= w−η∇L2(w). Then, we have L1(w′) −L1(w) ≤ϵ. Hence, the one-step forgetting is small if we have near- orthogonal gradients for the two tasks. The next question is whether widening the network increases the gradient orthog- onality. Empirically, to study the directions of the gradients for different tasks, in Figure 3, we plot the angle between the gradient vector at the minimum of the ﬁrst task and that of the subsequent tasks for various width factors. For this ﬁgure, we concatenate the gradients from all the layers into one vector. Lazy Training Regime In the previous two sections, we showed that the amount of forgetting induced by a single gradient descent step on a new task can be reduced by increased gradient orthogonal- ity/sparsity. In this section, we take a different perspective and study the entire training process of a task. In the fol- lowing, we denote by win t and w∗ t the initial and end model parameters for task t, respectively. Note that in the continual learning scenario, the initializer for a subsequent task is in fact the solution to the previous task. Thus, win t = w∗ t−1. Let us consider the amount of forgetting of task t−1 at the end of the training of taskt, measured by the increase in loss function Lt−1, i.e., Lt−1(w∗ t) −Lt−1(w∗ t−1). Suppose that the loss function is differentiable, by mean value theorem, there exists ξ∈[0,1] such that Lt−1(w∗ t) −Lt−1(w∗ t−1) =∇Lt−1((1 −ξ)w∗ t−1 + ξw∗ t)⊤(w∗ t −w∗ t−1), which yields the following upper bound on the amount of forgetting: Lt−1(w∗ t) −Lt−1(w∗ t−1) ≤Dt sup {w:∥w−w∗ t−1∥2≤Dt} ∥∇Lt−1(w)∥2, (4.2) where Dt := ∥w∗ t −w∗ t−1∥2 is the distance the the model parameter moves during the training of task t. This result suggests the following intuitive claim: The forgetting may be less severe if the model moves a shorter distance Dt in the parameter space. Interestingly, for overparametrized neural networks, the dis- tance that the model parameter moves during SGD training can indeed be small. In their seminal papers, Jacot et al. (2018) and Lee et al. (2019) connect learning in neural net- works to kernel methods and show that at the inﬁnite width limit, the kernel doesn’t change throughout the training, and the neural network evolves as a linear model under SGD training. Moreover, Chizat et al. (2019) show that these neural networks operate in lazy regime where ∥w∗−win∥2 is very small. Since wider networks are closer to the inﬁnite width limit, the moving distance Dt may be smaller for wider networks and thus the forgetting is less severe. To conﬁrm this intuition, in Figure 5, we plot the distance between the optimum of the ﬁrst task and that of the subse- quent tasks as the continual learning experience progress. In the ﬁgure, each task is trained for 5 epochs. From the ﬁgure, it can be seen that, for both MLPs and ResNets, the relative distance of the parameters for the wider networks is sub- stantially smaller than that of the less wide networks. This conﬁrms that lazy training of wider networks is indeed ben- eﬁcial for continual learning and reduces forgetting signiﬁ- cantly. In the same vein, Mirzadeh et al. (2020b;a) observed that changing the learning regime (i.e., imposing a learning rate decay, decreasing batch size, employing dropout, etc.) also leads to a small change in parameters from the optimum of previous tasks resulting in less forgetting. However, their work was concerned about the optimization properties of neural networks rather than architectural ones. 4.4. In fact, we observe that with increasing depth, the forgetting increases, as shown in Figure 2. We now provide an intuitive analysis for why and when the network depth hurts the performance of a continual learning model. Inspired by the exploding gradients phenomena in recurrent neural networks (Bengio et al., 1994; Pascanu et al., 2013), we show that deeper networks may cause larger gradient updates in the earlier layers. Larger gradients mean that the solution for the subsequent tasks will not be found in the vicinity of the current task, which would entail increased forgetting. Discussion and Conclusion In this paper, we studied a previously unexplored connec- tion between the width of the network and catastrophic forgetting (CF)—an important bottleneck for continual learning (CL) systems. Through different experiments, we hypothesize that high orthogonality between the gradients of different tasks induced by the wider networks, increased gradient sparsity, and a lazy training regime, i.e., the decreased distance of updated parameters from their initialization are the main factors alleviating catas- trophic forgetting. We highlighted the contrasts between over-parametrization with increasing width to increasing depth and argued that increasing depth might have negative consequences for forgetting while acknowledging its importance for learning representations. The scope of current work is to show a surprising and, at the same time, very intuitive correlation between width and forgetting. One should be cautious of utilizing increasing width to tackle catastrophic forgetting as it is undoubtedly an inefﬁcient decision in terms of computation time, energy and cost. By showing the connection between width and CF, our purpose here is to enhance our basic understanding of how over-parametrization, both in terms of width and depth, interacts with catastrophic forgetting. The extent of over-parametrization should be an important factor when designing continual learning benchmarks. We hope this work acts as a stepping stone for studying the interaction between the inherent properties of neural networks and catastrophic forgetting. In addition to vary- ing architecture sizes, modern neural networks employ sev- eral training tricks that are not well studied with respect to catastrophic forgetting. Understanding these effects, such as activation functions, normalization schemes, skip con- nections, etc., remains an interesting future work. Very recently, Mirzadeh et al. (2022) have studied the signiﬁ- cance of architectures in continual learning. They have extended our main results for other architectures (e.g., Vi- sion Transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021)) on large-scale benchmarks. In addition, they show that the role of ar- chitecture in continual learning can be as important as the algorithms, which suggests the intersection of continual learning and neural network architecture is an interesting and under-explored research direction. Experimental Setup Details In this section, we discuss our experimental setup, including the design choices for benchmarks, architectures, and hyper- parameters. A.1. Design Choices BENCHMARKS We have chosen the rotated MNIST benchmark since it is a common benchmark in the research literature and, unlike the permuted MNIST, has a meaningful shift across tasks. The number of 5 tasks on MNIST is also typical in the literature (Farajtabar et al., 2020; Mirzadeh et al., 2020b). While the rotation of 10 degrees per task is more common in the literature, we have increased the rotation to 22.5 degrees per task make the benchmark more difﬁcult and the performance gap between different models become more visible (Mirzadeh et al., 2021). While the rotated MNIST benchmark is domain-incremental, we have chosen the split CIFAR-100, which is a common task-incremental benchmark in the literature. Moreover, the split CIFAR-100 has 20 tasks, which helps support our arguments when the number of tasks increases. Our goal was to show our results in various setups such as domain versus task incremental, small versus large number of tasks, and single-head versus multi-head learning. ARCHITECTURES On the MNIST benchmark, MLP is a popular architecture in the literature (Wortsman et al., 2020; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). However, on the split CIFAR-100, ResNet-18 is a more popular choice (Chaudhry et al., 2021; Mirzadeh et al., 2021). However, WideResNets (WRN) have two essential properties that are more suitable for this study: ﬁrst, they share similar architectural properties with ResNets (e.g., skip-connections, batch normalization layers, etc.), and second, they have the nice property of ease of scaling both width and depth. We note that for the experiments that involved increasing depth, we have not chosen the thinnest models as a starting point. For instance, in Fig. 2, we have used MLP with a width of 128 and WideResNet with a width of 2. The reason is to make sure that the models are not too small, so by increasing the depth, the number of parameters increases in a meaningful manner. A.2. Hyperparameters For all experiments, we use a grid to ensure that one speciﬁc set of hyper-parameters is not favoring a speciﬁc model. Moreover, the training regime plays an important role in continual learning performance (Mirzadeh et al., 2020b). 1. learning rate: [0.001, 0.01 (MNIST), 0.05 (CIFAR), 0.1] 2. batch size: [16, 32 (CIFAR), 64 (MLP)] 3. SGD momentum: [0.0 (MNIST), 0.8 (CIFAR)] 4. weight decay: [0.0 (MNIST), 0.0001 (CIFAR)] For each set of hyper-parameters, we run the model using 5 different seeds for random initialization of the models. Moreover, to ensure that the speciﬁc ordering of tasks in the split CIFAR-100 is not playing a role in the results, we also use 3 additional seeds to shufﬂe the ordering of tasks.Wide Neural Networks Forget Less Catastrophically B. Task Construction in Claim 4.1 Consider a learning problem where the input space is Rd and the output space is R, and two model classes, F1,F2 ⊆ {Rd ↦→R}, where F1 is parameterized by w∈Rd: F1 := {fw : fw(x) = ⟨x,w⟩,w ∈Rd}, and F2 is parameterized by U ∈Rh×d and v∈Rh: F2 := {f : fU,v(x) = v⊤Ux,U ∈Rh×d,v ∈Rh}. This means that F1 is the set of linear models, and F2 is the set of two-layer linear networks. Clearly, we have F1 = F2, i.e., they have the same capacity, since there is no non-linearity used inF2. For any model f ∈F1 or F2, and data point (x,y) ∈Rd ×R, we use the quadratic loss function ℓ(f; x,y) = 1 2 (y−f(x))2. Now consider two tasks with training data points {(x1,i,y1,i)}n i=1 and {(x2,i,y2,i)}n i=1. We denote by Xt = [xt,i···xt,n]⊤ ∈Rn×d and Yt = [ yt,i···yt,n]⊤ ∈Rn the data matrix and label vector for task t (t = 1 ,2), respec- tively. The learner then trains the model with data for task 2. Let f2 be the model that the learner obtains after training on task 2. The forgetting metric is deﬁned as fgt(f2,f1) := L1(f2) −L1(f1). Then we train the model on task 2 using gradient descent for T steps with learning rate η. Let w0 and wT be the initial and end parameters for model class F1 in task 2 training, respectively, and let (U0,v0), (UT,vT) be the initial and end parameters for model class F2 in task 2 training, respectively. Then we have the following claim. Claim C.1(Claim 4.1 restated). There exist two tasks such that when we train task 2 using T steps of gradient descent, if we use model class F1, the amount of forgetting is strictly zero, i.e., fgt(fwT ,fw0 ) = 0; whereas if we use model class F2, the amount of forgetting can be positive, i.e., fgt(fUT ;vT ,fU0,v0 ) ≥0. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: This research investigates the impact of neural network architecture, specifically width and depth, on catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. The main problem addressed is the limited understanding of intrinsic neural network properties that contribute to catastrophic forgetting, beyond just continual learning algorithms. The key findings demonstrate that increasing the width of a neural network significantly reduces catastrophic forgetting, while increasing depth does not, and can even have negative effects. This reduction in forgetting is attributed to increased gradient orthogonality, increased gradient sparsity, and the network operating in a lazy training regime where parameters move shorter distances. The study also shows that the benefits of increased width are additive to existing continual learning algorithms.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The study primarily uses an empirical approach to analyze the relationship between network width/depth and catastrophic forgetting. For analysis, the learning dynamics of networks are studied from various perspectives: 1. Gradient Orthogonality: The angle between gradient vectors of different tasks is measured to see how orthogonality evolves with increasing width, hypothesizing that more orthogonal gradients lead to less forgetting. 2. Gradient Sparsity: The distribution of gradient magnitudes is analyzed, suggesting that sparser gradients (fewer parameters needing updates) reduce forgetting. 3. Lazy Training Regime: The distance moved by model parameters during the training of subsequent tasks (Euclidean distance between task optima) is measured, connecting smaller distances to the lazy training regime observed in over-parameterized networks. 4. Depth Analysis: The paper provides an intuitive analysis for the negative effects of depth, drawing parallels with exploding gradients in recurrent neural networks to explain larger gradient updates in earlier layers of deeper networks. The models used include Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLP) and WideResNets (WRN), trained with the SGD optimizer.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The research employs two standard continual learning benchmarks: Rotated MNIST (5 domain-incremental tasks, with rotations of 0, 22.5, 45, 67.5, and 90 degrees) and Split CIFAR-100 (20 task-incremental tasks, each with 5 random classes). For Rotated MNIST, a two-layer MLP with ReLU non-linearities is used, varying widths from 32 to 2048. For Split CIFAR-100, a WideResNet with a depth of 10 is used, varying width factors (multipliers for convolutional channels) by {1, 2, 4, 8}. All models are trained for five epochs per task using the SGD optimizer, with hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, SGD momentum, weight decay) optimized via a grid search. Results are reported as average and standard deviation over five runs with different random seeds for network initialization. For Split CIFAR-100, three additional seeds are used for random task ordering. Evaluation metrics include Average Accuracy, Average Forgetting (difference between peak and final accuracy), Learning Accuracy (accuracy immediately after learning a task), and Joint Accuracy (accuracy of a model trained on all data simultaneously). Additional experiments explored interaction with CL algorithms like ER, A-GEM, MC-SGD, LwF, and EWC, and comparisons of models with fixed parameter counts.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The paper acknowledges that using increased width to tackle catastrophic forgetting is computationally inefficient, energy-intensive, and costly. Its primary purpose is to enhance fundamental understanding, not to propose a practical state-of-the-art solution. The intuitive analysis for why increasing depth might be detrimental (related to exploding gradients) is noted as a potential scenario rather than a strict theoretical proof, especially when singular values of intermediate weight matrices are greater than 1, making the theoretical bound loose. The study also does not extensively delve into optimization strategies designed to mitigate issues like exploding gradients, instead using the phenomenon to explain observed effects.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future research directions include further studying the interaction between the inherent properties of neural networks and catastrophic forgetting. Investigating the effects of various modern training tricks and architectural components (such as activation functions, normalization schemes, and skip connections) on catastrophic forgetting is suggested. The paper highlights the intersection of continual learning and neural network architecture as an interesting and underexplored research direction. Additionally, a more detailed study into why certain continual learning algorithms (e.g., MC-SGD, LwF) show greater benefits from increased width compared to others is proposed. Finally, the extent of over-parametrization should be considered an important factor when designing future continual learning benchmarks.
